summary: Defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for managing DS1, E1, DS2 and E2 interfaces, the digital trunk lines (such as T1 and E1) used by carriers and enterprises. Network management tools use it over SNMP to monitor and configure those lines. It was replaced by RFC 3895.

plainLanguage.summary: Big digital phone lines need a checkup. This document is a standard form listing what to measure on them, like errors and whether they are working, so any monitoring program can read it from any maker's equipment.

subtitle: Management information base for digital trunk lines and their performance

tldr.problem: Digital trunk lines (T1, E1, etc.) need to be monitored and managed by network operators, but there was no standard way to access and report their configuration and performance statistics via SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2495 defines a MIB module with managed objects for DS1, E1, DS2, and E2 interfaces, including configuration tables, error counters, performance parameters collected in 15-minute intervals, and loopback testing capabilities.
tldr.outcome: Network management tools can now uniformly query and configure these digital interfaces across different vendor equipment, though it was replaced by RFC 3895 for updated definitions.

today: RFC 2495 defined SNMP management objects for DS1/E1/DS2/E2 interfaces and was obsoleted by RFC 3895. However, the concepts and terminology remain foundational to telecommunications line management.

sections.title: Digital Trunk Lines and SNMP Management
sections.content:
DS1, E1, DS2, and E2 are digital transmission interfaces used by telephone companies and enterprises to carry voice and data over long distances. In North America, the DS1 (also called T1) operates at 1.544 megabits per second. The E1 is the European equivalent at 2.048 Mbps. DS2 and E2 are higher-speed variants at 6.312 Mbps and 8.448 Mbps respectively. These lines are fundamental infrastructure in telecommunications networks.

Network operators need to monitor these lines for errors, measure their performance, and adjust their configuration. RFC 2495 defines how SNMP management stations can access and control these interfaces through standardized managed objects organized into a Management Information Base (MIB).
sections.plainLanguage: Digital phone lines are highways for data and voice. Managers need to check if they work, how many errors happen on them, and be able to test them or reroute traffic. A standard checklist lets any company's monitoring software read the same information from equipment from any vendor.

sections.title: MIB Structure and Object Groups
sections.content:
The DS1/E1 MIB module defines five main groups of managed objects. The Configuration Table contains writable parameters such as line type (D4, ESF, CRC, no CRC), signal encoding method, loopback configuration, and cable length. The Current Table holds real-time performance statistics like errors and defects currently being experienced. The Interval Table stores performance data collected over 15-minute periods, with up to 96 intervals (24 hours) kept by the agent.

The Total Table maintains a rolling 24-hour total of each performance parameter. The Far End Table contains information about errors and defects detected by the remote equipment and sent back via the digital signal itself. The Fractional Table (now deprecated) allowed configuration of sub-channel groups for channelization, breaking one DS1 into multiple DS0 channels.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB is organized into groups that store different kinds of information: what the line is set up to do, how it is performing right now, its performance over the last 24 hours in 15-minute chunks, and what errors the far end is reporting.

sections.title: Error Events and Performance Defects
sections.content:
RFC 2495 defines standard terminology for errors on digital lines based on the ANSI T1.231 standard. Bipolar Violation errors occur when adjacent signal pulses have the same polarity instead of alternating, indicating corruption of the signal. Line Coding Violations include both bipolar violations and excessive zeroes (more than 15 contiguous zero bits in AMI-coded signals, or more than 7 in B8ZS-coded signals).

Path Coding Violations are frame synchronization bit errors or CRC errors that indicate problems in the framing structure. Out of Frame defects are declared when the receiver detects too many framing errors within a short time window, causing the framer to lose synchronization. Alarm Indication Signal (AIS) defects are detected as an 'all ones' condition on the line, typically sent by the remote end to indicate a loss of signal.

Controlled Slip events occur when timing differences cause the deletion or replication of payload bits. Each of these events is counted separately to provide diagnostic information about the nature of line problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Errors are counted in different categories—signal timing problems, framing problems, and loss-of-signal alarms. Managers see not just 'errors happened' but what kind of errors, helping diagnose whether the problem is in the cable, the framing format, or something else.

sections.title: Performance Parameters and Monitoring
sections.content:
Performance parameters are collected continuously in 15-minute intervals and accumulated into several counters. Errored Seconds count seconds in which one or more errors were detected. Line Errored Seconds specifically count seconds with line coding violations. Severely Errored Seconds indicate seconds with very high error rates (320 or more path coding violations in ESF format), or out-of-frame defects, or detected AIS.

Bursty Errored Seconds (ESF only) are seconds with moderate errors (between 2 and 319 path coding violations) without severe defects. Controlled Slip Seconds count seconds in which controlled slips occurred. Degraded Minutes are one-minute intervals where the estimated error rate exceeds 1 millionth per bit but remains below 1 thousandth per bit (between 1E-6 and 1E-3).

Unavailable Seconds occur when the interface is down or in an out-of-frame condition. All these parameters accumulate over 15-minute intervals and are also totaled over a rolling 24-hour period, allowing operators to detect trends and long-term problems.
sections.plainLanguage: The system counts seconds with errors of different severity levels (a few errors versus many), plus minutes where overall performance is degraded. 96 intervals of 15 minutes each give you 24 hours of history to see if the line is getting worse.

sections.title: Operational Uses and Loopback Testing
sections.content:
The MIB supports several operational tasks. Managers can query the configuration table to verify line type, encoding, and other settings. They can read current and historical performance data to diagnose problems and confirm that quality metrics meet service agreements.

One important capability is loopback testing. A manager can request that the interface enter loopback mode, where transmitted data is looped back to the receiver, allowing the equipment to test that the local hardware is working correctly. Types of loopback include line loopback (loops back at the line interface), payload loopback (loops back the payload data), inward loopback (loops back at the input), and dual loopback (combination of line and inward). The remote end can also request loopback via the Facility Data Link (FDL) channel in ESF format.

The MIB also supports channelization, where a DS3 interface can be divided into multiple DS2 or DS1 channels, and DS1 can be divided into DS0 channels. The Channel Mapping Table tracks these relationships.
sections.plainLanguage: Managers can reconfigure lines, run loopback tests to check if their own equipment is working, and track performance over time to prove the line meets its service contract.
